stories.title: Fed minutes: nearly all officials see more hikes ahead
chain: Minutes of the October meeting came out at 2pm ET
Nearly all officials saw further hikes as likely appropriate
December hike odds stay around 92%, and a bigger move is discussed
Stocks reversed a small gain, the dollar rose, gold fell

depth.simple: Every few weeks the Fed publishes notes on what its officials said behind closed doors. This time the notes showed that almost everyone thinks interest rates will probably need to go higher to bring inflation down. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and make shares and gold look less attractive. Stocks gave up a small gain after the notes came out.
depth.standard: The minutes of the 27-28 October meeting, released on 18 November, showed that nearly all officials judged further rate increases would likely be appropriate. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack had voted for a quarter-point hike in October. CME FedWatch put the odds of a 25bp hike on 8-9 December at about 92%. The S&P 500 reversed a modest gain after the release and closed down 0.23% at 7,323.63, a fifth straight loss. Reports also point to comments from Waller about a possible bigger December move. The 10-year yield still ended slightly lower at 5.07%.
depth.pro: The minutes confirm a broad hawkish consensus, so the live question is the size and number of hikes, not December itself. Reports of Waller floating a half-point move raise the tail risk on the terminal rate. The 10-year ended down 4bp at 5.07%, which suggests the curve had already priced much of this, while the dollar index rose 0.36% and gold fell. Equity multiples face pressure from real yields. Watch Fed speakers (Hammack on Thursday) and the pricing of the 2027 path.

stories.title: Anthropic prices its IPO at $83, above range; trading starts today
chain: Demand ran several times above the shares offered
The price was set at $83, above the $70-78 range
About $81 billion raised, a record for an IPO
ANT starts trading on Nasdaq today, Thursday 19 Nov

depth.simple: Anthropic sold its shares to the public for the first time and set the price at $83 each. That is above the range it first suggested, because many more investors wanted shares than were available. It raised about $81 billion, the most ever for a stock market debut. Its shares start trading today under the ticker ANT.
depth.standard: The IPO priced on 18 November at $83, above the $70-78 range, raising about $81.3 billion and valuing the company at roughly $1.5 trillion, according to reports. Roughly 956 million shares were sold by the company and 23.65 million by co-founders, and a separate $26 billion private placement brings the total to about $107 billion (CNN). Underwriters have a 30-day option on up to 147 million more shares. The offering is expected to close on 20 November. One Morningstar analyst put fair value at $92. Asian stocks did not rally on the news.
depth.pro: Pricing above range with heavy oversubscription points to scarcity of AI supply, but the size matters: roughly $81B of new paper has to be absorbed in a falling tape with a hawkish Fed. The greenshoe adds stabilisation capacity. Watch the opening auction, day-one volume, whether suppliers who invested in the deal (the circular-funding worry) are hit, and read-across to Nvidia, which reversed its post-earnings gain on Wednesday.

stories.title: Nvidia gives back its post-earnings gain, down 2.9%
chain: Nvidia beat forecasts and guided to about $130B
Shares rose early, then reversed
Worries about AI spending and Huang's exit stayed in focus
Fell about 2.9%, while the Nasdaq still rose 0.42%

depth.simple: Nvidia's results were strong on Tuesday, and the shares first rose. On Wednesday they gave up the gain and fell about 2.9%. Investors still worry about how long AI spending can grow and about the company's leadership change. Even so, the wider Nasdaq index ended higher.
depth.standard: After reporting revenue of $115.8B and guiding to about $130B for next quarter, Nvidia reversed an early gain on 18 November and fell about 2.9%. The Nasdaq Composite still gained 0.42% to 24,429.88, helped by AI sentiment ahead of the Anthropic pricing, while the Dow fell 1.11% to 50,198.17. In Asia, Korea's Kospi closed up 1.99% on Wednesday on the outlook, and is up another 0.46% today.
depth.pro: The reversal after a clean beat and a raised guide shows positioning and macro, not fundamentals, driving the tape: de-grossing, higher real rates and the leadership overhang. A strong print that fails to hold is a classic sign that the good news was priced in. Watch gross margin commentary, the Rubin ramp, and whether Anthropic's debut pulls flows into or out of the suppliers.

stories.title: Gold falls to a 14-month low as the dollar and yields rise
chain: Fed hike odds rose and the dollar firmed
Real yields rose, so holding gold costs more
Gold fell about 3% in one day
It broke below $3,800, a 14-month low

depth.simple: Gold pays no interest. When interest rates rise, safe savings pay more, so gold looks less attractive. A stronger dollar also makes gold dearer for buyers using other currencies. Both happened on Wednesday, and gold dropped to its lowest price in over a year.
depth.standard: Gold futures closed at $3,741.90, down 3.16% on the day, after spot gold broke below $3,800 and hit a 14-month low. Silver fell about 3%. The dollar index rose 0.36% to 103.86. CME FedWatch showed about a 92% chance of a December hike, and hawkish remarks from Fed officials added to the move. Exact spot levels vary by time of day between sources.
depth.pro: Gold is trading as a real-yield and dollar instrument, not a safe haven: it fell even as stocks wobbled and Gulf risks continued. The move through $3,800 likely triggered technical selling and long liquidation. Falling oil and copper also point to a broader commodity unwind. Watch the dollar, TIPS real yields, and ETF outflows.

stories.title: European stocks fall again as miners and energy slide
chain: Copper hit a seven-month low and oil fell
Mining stocks dropped 4.7%, the most since May
Caution built ahead of the Anthropic IPO

depth.simple: European shares fell for a second day. Mining companies dropped sharply because copper got cheaper, and oil companies fell with oil. Investors also did not want to take big risks before Anthropic's share sale. Spain's IBEX 35 lost 1.28%.
depth.standard: The STOXX 600 fell 1.03% to 644.05 after Tuesday's 1.75% drop, its biggest in eight months. Spain's IBEX 35 lost 1.28% to 19,373.30, Germany's DAX 1.19% to 25,736.24 and the Euro Stoxx 50 0.93% to 6,154.39. Miners fell 4.7% as copper hit a seven-month low. Oil stocks lost 2.1%. Alstom fell 7.2% after a net loss of €822 million.
depth.pro: The sell-off is cyclical as well as AI-driven: copper at a seven-month low and a firm dollar point to a global growth scare layered on top of hawkish central banks. The IBEX, heavy in banks and energy, normally benefits from higher rates but was hit by energy and commodity exposure. Watch whether the ECB tone hardens and whether Europe's two-day drop turns into a trend.

stories.title: Brent slips to $92 even as Iran threats and tanker attacks continue
chain: Tanker attacks and Trump's strike threat keep risk alive
Gulf exports and Hormuz traffic have mostly recovered
A Q4 surplus and rising US stockpiles weigh on prices
Brent fell 1.28% to $91.95

depth.simple: Oil usually jumps when there is danger in the Gulf. This time it did not. Ships are moving through the area again, the world is expected to have more oil than it needs, and US stockpiles are rising. So Brent drifted down to about $92 a barrel, even though attacks on tankers go on.
depth.standard: Brent closed at $91.95, down 1.28%, and WTI fell 3.2% to $83.26. Iran's navy says three tankers east of Hormuz were disabled by mines, and Trump was reported to be weighing action with Israel. Traffic data is mixed: one tracker shows few transits, while CNBC cites near pre-war flows. Goldman forecasts $105 Brent in December, while others see a slide towards $87-88.
depth.pro: The risk premium is being fought by physical balances: a forecast Q4 surplus, swelling US inventories and workarounds around the Strait. The wider Brent-WTI spread suggests US-specific bearishness on stocks. Escalation would show up first in war-risk insurance and freight, not spot price. For Europe, lower oil eases the ECB's energy-driven inflation concern.

stories.title: Dow falls 848 points as software stocks lead a fourth losing day
chain: Software and tech stocks sold off before Nvidia reported
Salesforce -9.45%; every S&P 500 sector fell
S&P 500 -1.03%, its lowest close since late July
Investors waited for Nvidia before deciding what comes next

depth.simple: US stocks fell for a fourth day. The Dow lost 848 points, or 1.6%. Software companies were hit hardest: Salesforce dropped almost 10%. Many investors did not want to hold risky tech shares before Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom, reported its results after the close.
depth.standard: The S&P 500 closed at 7,340.53 (-1.03%), its lowest close since late July. The Dow fell 848.75 points (-1.64%) to 50,759.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.74% to 24,328.38 after sliding as much as 2.1% during the day. All sectors fell; financials were weakest. Salesforce closed down 9.45% at $194.52. Nvidia itself barely moved in regular trading (about -0.4%).
depth.pro: The move was broader than Monday's chip-led drop: software and financials led, which points to de-grossing and a higher discount rate rather than a single-name story. The Nasdaq's recovery from a 2.1% intraday low shows dip buyers into the print. With the 10-year already above 5% and a December Fed hike priced as near-certain, long-duration equity multiples stay under pressure. Watch whether the Nvidia beat lifts the wider tape or only chipmakers.

stories.title: Nvidia beats and guides to $130 billion, shares rise after hours
chain: Nvidia reports its first quarter without Jensen Huang
Revenue $115.8B vs about $109B expected
Q4 guidance near $130B vs about $125B expected
Shares rise 3-5% after hours; Asian chip stocks react this morning

depth.simple: Nvidia reported its first results since its founder-CEO Jensen Huang resigned. Sales were about $115.8 billion, double a year earlier and well above forecasts. It also said sales next quarter should be about $130 billion. That calmed investors, and the shares rose in after-hours trading.
depth.standard: Revenue for the quarter to 25 October was $115.84B (+103% year on year) against about $109B expected. Adjusted EPS was $2.68 vs $2.47-2.48. Fourth-quarter revenue guidance is about $130B versus a $125.1B consensus (LSEG). Reports say the company raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to 75% from 70%. The board does not plan to bring Huang back. After-hours gains were reported at roughly 3-5%; sources differ on the exact figure.
depth.pro: The beat answers the fundamental question, but the stock has fallen about 16% since the scandal broke, so the debate is now governance and key-person risk rather than demand. Gross margin guidance (reported at 71-72%) and the Rubin ramp are the watch items. Asia's muted reaction, with the leadership and spy-affair headlines still in focus, shows that a strong print does not remove the overhang. Whether Wednesday's session holds the after-hours gain is the open question.

depth.simple: Anthropic is selling shares to the public for the first time. It sets the final price tonight and trading starts Thursday under the ticker ANT. Reports say investors asked for about six times the shares available, so some may price above the planned range of $70 to $78.
depth.standard: The range is $70-78 for 825 million Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. At the top end that implies about $1.4 trillion fully diluted; on shares outstanding, estimates are about $0.9-1.0 trillion. CNBC cited sources saying the deal may price above range. Final pricing is expected on 18 Nov. Nothing has been confirmed at the time of writing.
depth.pro: Strong demand into a falling tape makes this a test of risk appetite for AI paper. Pricing above range would signal that supply, not demand, is scarce; it also raises first-day expectations, which the call below tests. Watch allocation behaviour, the circular-funding concern from supplier investors, and whether a rebounding Nvidia helps the debut.

stories.title: Fed minutes today; ECB also leans towards a December hike
chain: October CPI came in hotter than forecast
Fed held rates but two members voted to hike (10-2)
Markets price about 92-96% odds of a December hike
Minutes at 2pm ET show how broad the hawkish camp is

depth.simple: Central banks are leaning towards raising interest rates again because inflation is stubborn. The Fed releases notes from its October meeting at 2pm New York time. Two officials already wanted a hike then, and traders think a hike in December is almost certain. In Europe, the ECB's president has also said a hike is possible.
depth.standard: The Fed held its target range at 3.75-4.00% on 28 Oct in a 10-2 vote; Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented in favour of a quarter-point rise. The next meeting is 8-9 Dec, with CME FedWatch showing roughly 92-96% odds of a 25bp hike. Waller has backed a December hike. In the euro area, Lagarde said on 7-8 Nov that inflation will stay high and driven by energy, and that a December hike could follow.
depth.pro: The minutes matter for breadth and pace: how many officials see a hike as warranted, and whether anyone talks about a series rather than one move. With a December hike priced in, the surprise risk is on the terminal-rate path, not December. A more hawkish read would pressure long-duration assets and support the dollar. For the ECB the energy pass-through is the mechanism; oil staying lower would ease the case.

stories.title: Oil steadies as US-Iran talks stall and Gulf attacks continue
chain: On-and-off US-Iran talks fail to settle the conflict
Attacks on Gulf shipping continue
Oil swings in a $3 range but holds near Monday's level
A forecast Q4 supply surplus caps the rally

depth.simple: Oil prices were steady on Tuesday after Monday's big drop. Talks between the US and Iran keep starting and stopping, and attacks on ships in the Gulf go on. But the world is expected to have more oil than it needs this quarter, which keeps a lid on prices.
depth.standard: Brent swung in a range of about $3 and ended near the previous day's level, with reports of afternoon settlements around $93. The IEA said last week the market should turn to surplus in Q4. Iran's restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz and tanker strikes remain the main upside risk. Exact settlement levels vary between sources.
depth.pro: The market is pricing a risk premium against a surplus. Escalation in the Strait would hit tanker insurance and freight before it hits physical supply, so watch war-risk premiums and UKMTO notices. A deal would remove the premium quickly, while a surplus means downside needs less help than upside.

stories.title: Nasdaq drops 2.5% as Nvidia turmoil and chip curbs hit tech
chain: Nvidia leaderless, new US chip-export rules
Nvidia −4.1%, chip stocks sold
Tonight's Nvidia earnings carry even more weight

depth.simple: US stocks had a bad Monday, with the Nasdaq (heavy in tech) down 2.5%. Investors are nervous about Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom. It lost its founder-CEO last week and Washington added new limits on selling advanced chips abroad. Nvidia reports its results tonight, so many investors sold first and waited for answers.
depth.standard: The S&P 500 closed at 7,416.59 (−1.92%), the Nasdaq at 24,509.76 (−2.49%) and the Dow at 51,608.17 (−1.41%), a third straight losing day. The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, rose about 19%. Nvidia fell about 4.1%. Nvidia has guided to revenue of about $108 billion for the quarter, plus or minus 2%. Analysts will focus less on that number than on the outlook and on how interim CEO Colette Kress handles questions about leadership.
depth.pro: The selloff combines three overlapping risks: key-person risk at the sector's bellwether, a regulatory shock to the addressable market (new licensing in five countries plus remote-access limits), and a rate backdrop above 5% on the 10-year that compresses long-duration multiples. Rising VIX into a binary event means options are expensive, so the post-earnings move may be large either way. Positioning matters: after a three-day drop, a clean guide could trigger a sharp relief rally, while any cut to the roadmap or China commentary would confirm the de-rating.

stories.title: Washington tightens AI-chip export rules, closing the cloud loophole
chain: Commerce issues interim rule
Licences needed for chips to five more countries
Remote access for Chinese firms also covered
Nvidia's China-linked demand faces more uncertainty

depth.simple: The US government said companies now need a licence to send advanced AI chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. It also limits Chinese firms from renting that computing power remotely through foreign data centres. The aim is to stop China getting chips through the back door. For Nvidia, it adds another worry on top of its leadership crisis.
depth.standard: The Commerce Department's interim rule covers exports and re-exports of advanced semiconductors to the five countries, and overseas data centres that give Chinese firms access to such chips now need federal licences. Operators already providing that capacity get 90 days after the rule takes effect to apply. Coverage links the move to the Nvidia scandal and to an upcoming meeting between Trump and Xi. Nvidia shares fell on the news. Some details of the Huang story rest on a few outlets and are still unsettled.
depth.pro: The significant change is the remote-access provision: it targets compute-as-a-service, not just hardware shipments, which is how a lot of China-linked demand had been routed through Southeast Asian data centres. Watch for how Nvidia sizes the revenue at risk on tonight's call, how Singapore- and Malaysia-based operators apply for licences, and whether Beijing retaliates around the Trump–Xi talks. Second-order effects hit server makers and memory suppliers in Asia, which fits this week's weakness in Kospi chip names.

stories.title: Anthropic IPO book reported about 6× covered, Nvidia to invest $10B
chain: 825M shares at $70–78
Order book reportedly ~6× the shares
Banks expect pricing could exceed the range
Day-one trading tests AI appetite after the selloff
stories.disclosure: This brief is written by Claude, which is made by Anthropic. It covers Anthropic like any other company and takes no view on buying the shares.

depth.simple: Anthropic plans to sell 825 million shares at $70–78 each. Reports say investors have asked for about six times as many shares as are on offer. That means many buyers will get less than they wanted, and the price could be set above the range. Nvidia has also agreed to buy about $10 billion of the shares. The company is expected to start trading Thursday, right after a rough day for tech stocks.
depth.standard: Pricing is expected Wednesday 18 November and trading from Thursday 19 November under the ticker ANT. At the top of the range the base deal raises about $64 billion. If priced higher and counting a private placement of about $26 billion across chip and cloud suppliers, reports say it could pass $100 billion and beat SpaceX's $85.7 billion IPO from June. The order book comes from Bloomberg via Reuters; banks have warned buyers of smaller allocations. Sources differ on the final timing, and no final price exists yet.
depth.pro: Oversubscription is not a guarantee of a first-day pop: heavily covered deals have a history of weak debuts, and one investor warned of that this week. A private placement from suppliers such as Nvidia and Google is also circular financing, since the money may flow back to them as chip and cloud spending. If shares trade below the IPO price, those investors hold paper losses. Beyond day one, the share count, lock-up expiries and the supply of new stock for funds to absorb will matter more for the medium-term price.

stories.title: Warsh talks about an AI bubble, a December hike stays on the table
chain: Warsh: Fed staff studying AI-bubble risk
No hint on rates
10-year yield ~5.1%, hike seen near-certain
Higher yields keep pressure on tech valuations

depth.simple: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh spoke at an event on AI and the economy. He said Fed economists are studying whether an AI bubble could burst and how AI affects jobs. He did not comment on interest rates. Markets still expect the Fed to raise rates in December, which keeps the US 10-year yield near 5.1%. When safe bonds pay that much, expensive stocks look riskier.
depth.standard: Warsh said productivity growth is reasonably strong but has not broken out yet, which implies AI's big payoff is still ahead. He gave no comment on recent price moves or the near-term inflation path. Futures see a December hike as close to certain, and the Fed's October minutes come out Wednesday. The 10-year yield is around 5.12–5.14% across sources, and yields eased a little Monday after a bruising week.
depth.pro: The notable signal is that the Fed chair is publicly framing AI-bubble risk as a research topic, which markets could read as the Fed adding financial stability to its list of worries. For rates, the debate is whether the hiking cycle extends past December: core inflation is running near 3.7% annualised. Watch the minutes for how many officials wanted a hike in October and the term premium, since falling equity prices alone will not stop the Fed if inflation stays hot.

stories.title: Oil falls 3.6% as Hormuz flows recover, despite new tanker reports
chain: Hormuz shipping flows recover
IEA sees a Q4 supply surplus
Lower energy costs ease inflation pressure at the margin

depth.simple: Oil fell on Monday even though Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Reuters could not verify that claim. Traders focused on oil flowing again and on a forecast that the world will have more oil than it needs this quarter. Cheaper oil is good news for inflation.
depth.standard: Brent settled at $92.44 (−3.6%) and WTI at $85.72 (−3.2%), per Reuters. The IEA said the market should return to surplus in the fourth quarter. Vice President Vance said President Trump would not let the Iran conflict turn into a prolonged war. Intraday prices earlier in the day were in the mid-$90s, so we use the settlement price.
depth.pro: The market is pricing flow data over headlines: recovering Gulf exports and an IEA surplus call outweigh unverified mine reports. A durable move lower in Brent would take pressure off headline CPI in the US and the euro area, where October inflation hit 4.0% on energy. The risk is asymmetry: if a confirmed incident closes the strait again, the curve would flip quickly back to steep backwardation.

stories.title: Nvidia loses its founder-CEO days before earnings
chain: Huang exits after a board probe
Leadership and China-security questions
Chip stocks sold worldwide
This week's earnings become a confidence test

depth.simple: Jensen Huang, who founded Nvidia and ran it for over 30 years, left as CEO last week after a board investigation into his personal conduct, which included reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia makes the chips behind most of the world's AI, so investors treat it as the barometer for the whole AI trade. Losing its leader just before it reports results pushed investors to sell chip stocks from New York to Seoul.
depth.standard: The board named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO and created an independent chair role, filled by Harvey Jones. The official wording is a resignation; CNBC's sources say the board pushed him out, and today report that the board is not considering bringing him back despite a petition and allies lobbying for it. Congressional committees may call him to testify. Nvidia had its worst week since the April 2025 tariff selloff, and the selling hit its Asian suppliers this morning: SK Hynix −7.9%, Kospi −3.6%. Monday's US session opened lower again, with Nasdaq 100 futures down; closing levels were still provisional in the sources we checked.
depth.pro: Two things drive the valuation question. First, key-person risk: Huang personally anchored the hyperscaler relationships and the credibility of the product roadmap. Second, a possible national-security angle that could tighten scrutiny of China-linked sales. Q3 consensus EPS is about $2.47–2.49. The quarter itself is largely locked in by orders already placed, so the market will trade the guidance and whether Kress can reassure on roadmap and customer commitments. A beat with soft guidance would likely be read as the start of a de-rating.

stories.title: The US 10-year yield breaks 5% as a December hike gets priced in
chain: October inflation runs hot (+0.4% m/m)
~92% odds of a Fed hike on 9 Dec
10-year yield: 4.86% → 5.15% in a week
Costlier borrowing, pressure on stock valuations

depth.simple: US inflation came in higher than expected in October, mostly because of energy. That makes it very likely the Federal Reserve raises interest rates again in December, after already raising them in September. When investors expect higher rates, government bond yields rise too. The 10-year US yield is the reference rate for mortgages and company borrowing around the world, and it is now above 5%. At that level, safe bonds become a serious alternative to stocks.
depth.standard: The Fed's range is 3.75–4.00% after a September hike under Chair Kevin Warsh and a hold on 28 October, when two members voted to hike. Futures price about 92% odds of +0.25 pts at the 8–9 December meeting and 8% odds of +0.50. Governor Waller has floated the bigger move. Warsh speaks today and the October minutes come out Wednesday. Stocks still rose on the week (S&P +2.5%), but fast-growing tech stocks are the most exposed if yields keep climbing, because more of their value sits in profits far in the future.
depth.pro: The 10-year added roughly 30bp in a week to about 5.15%. Core CPI has printed +0.3% m/m three months running, about 3.7% annualised, so the debate is the terminal rate, not the timing. Watch the term premium: if long yields keep rising after hikes are already priced, the driver is fiscal and supply worries rather than Fed expectations, which is worse for equity multiples. Note that the BLS did not publish a 12-month CPI rate because October 2025 data were never collected during the shutdown.

stories.title: Iran escalates in the Gulf: drones at Bahrain, tankers hit in Hormuz
chain: IRGC drones at a US radar site in Bahrain
Iran says 6 tankers hit since Sunday
Shipping risk up, but glut fears cap oil
Expensive energy keeps inflation sticky

depth.simple: Iran launched drones at a US military site in Bahrain over the weekend; Bahrain says it shot them all down. Iran also says several oil tankers were hit by mines or projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Oil is already expensive, with Brent around $96 a barrel, and that feeds the inflation pushing central banks to raise rates.
depth.standard: Iran has restricted passage through Hormuz and attacks ships it says break its rules. The UK's maritime agency (UKMTO) confirmed one vessel was hit, with all crew safe; Iran's claim that a supertanker sank is unverified. Reuters reports President Trump is weighing holding off on strikes unless there are new provocations. Oil actually eased this morning because the IEA's outlook revived worries about a global supply surplus, so the market is weighing disruption against weak demand.
depth.pro: Watch the oil futures curve and tanker rates rather than headline Brent: a real disruption shows up as steeper backwardation and a spike in freight. The second-order effect matters more. European gas has risen and Japan's Q3 contraction was blamed on energy costs, so energy is now a growth problem for importers (Europe, Japan, Korea) and an inflation problem for the Fed and the ECB at once. That stagflationary mix is the worst backdrop for long-duration equities.

stories.title: Anthropic lists this week: the biggest test yet of AI appetite
chain: 825M shares at $70–78
Raises up to ~$64B, the largest IPO ever
Prices Wed 18, trades Thu 19 (ANT)
The first-day move is a vote on AI valuations
stories.disclosure: This brief is written by Claude, which is made by Anthropic. It covers Anthropic like any other company and takes no view on buying the shares.

depth.simple: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, plans to list its shares on the Nasdaq this week. It wants to raise around $61–64 billion, which would make it by far the largest stock market debut ever. How the shares trade on day one will show how much investors still want to pay for AI right after the Nvidia shock.
depth.standard: Pricing is expected Wednesday 18 November, with trading from Thursday 19 November under the ticker ANT. The range values the company at up to about $1.4 trillion fully diluted, below the roughly $2 trillion some investors talked about over the summer. Reports say the banks are weighing a higher price, which would push the valuation to $1.5 trillion or more. Some analysts read the lower range as a deliberate choice to leave room for a first-day jump. Reports also say demand is strong (one outlet says the book is several times covered) and that Nvidia plans to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic ahead of the listing; sources differ on the raise size ($64B to $80B) and valuation ($1.3–1.5T).
depth.pro: Mind the share count. On about 13.1B basic shares the market cap is roughly $0.92–1.02T; the $1.3–1.4T headline includes options and restricted stock. A $60B+ raise is also a liquidity event: funds may trim other mega-cap AI holdings to make room, a supply overhang for the sector in the week it lists. For the medium-term price, lock-up expiries matter more than day one.

stories.title: Europe at records while Asia slides: the AI selloff is uneven
chain: Stoxx 600 record close, best week since June
Led by insurers and oil majors, not tech
Asia today: Kospi −3.6%, Nikkei −2.4%
Europe's low AI exposure works as a shelter

depth.simple: European stocks closed at another record on Friday and the IBEX 35 stayed above 20,000, while Asian markets fell hard this morning. The difference is what each market is made of. Korea and Taiwan are full of chipmakers that sell to Nvidia. Europe's indexes are heavy in banks, insurers and energy companies, which do fine when rates are high and oil is expensive.
depth.standard: The Stoxx 600 closed at 664.14, up 2.4% on the week, led by insurers and oil producers while chipmakers lagged (Infineon −4.3%). In Japan, data showed the economy contracted in the third quarter as energy costs bit, pulling the Nikkei down 2.4%. Euro-area inflation reached 4.0% in October, and most economists expect the ECB to raise its deposit rate in December as well.
depth.pro: Sector mix explains most of the gap. Europe is overweight financials, which earn more from lending when rates rise, and energy, and it is underweight semiconductors. The cushion has limits: an ECB hike into slowing growth and energy-led inflation is a stagflation setup, and the IBEX's heavy bank weighting makes it sensitive to any credit wobble. Korea and Taiwan's concentration in SK Hynix, Samsung and TSMC makes their indexes leveraged bets on AI spending.
